title: Cold-start KV slowpath profiling — lab diary
content:
Summary:
This is a lab diary for a short investigative spike to understand cold-start behavior for KV cache misses that fall into the slowpath (page population / DMA / swapback) and how those events amplify tail latency under multi-tenant mixed workloads. Goal was to produce reproducible traces, identify dominant microsecond/ms contributors, and propose low-risk mitigations we can A/B test on a Dedicated pool.

Why this matters:
- We see sporadic tail spikes (p99.9) on production serving nodes that correlate with new long-prefix sessions (cold KV residency). The surface-level symptom is increased per-request token latency for first few requests after a model/version change or a scaled-up worker.
- Customer impact: interactive chat apps and stream-first flows show visible lag during these tails.
- Hypothesis: cold-start slowpath is driven by a combination of page faults (hugepage/transparent hugepage behavior), non-sequential KV page access patterns, and brief memory bandwidth saturation from background prefetching/compaction.

Test environment and config:
- Hardware: 8x A100 (40GB) per worker; host OS Ubuntu 22.04; NVMe swapback configured for overflow experiments.
- Runtime: main branch at commit d2b9f3; local patches added to increase KV telemetry and enable fine-grained PCM counters.
- Workloads: synthetic replay of production trace (sampled), two variants: 1) heavy long-prefix sessions (seqlen 2048/avg), 2) mixed small/large sessions (avg seqlen 512).
- KV config: shard size 2GB, page size 64KB (experimentally tuned), default TTL 15m; cold-policy: lazy-load on demand; prefetch disabled initially.
- Instrumentation: perf+ebpf for kernel events, nvprof for DMA, per-page residency histograms, custom tracepoints for slowpath entry/exit, and per-request timeline (queueing/kv-miss/dma/pagefill/cpu-exec).

What we measured (representative numbers):
- Baseline (no background load): p50 token latency 28ms, p99 110ms, p99.9 320ms.
- Cold wave (simulated 500 new sessions over 30s): p50 35ms, p99 180ms, p99.9 1.1s.
- Kerneled page fault servicing time distribution: median 120us, 95th 2.4ms, 99.9th spikes up to 120ms when concurrent.
- DMA transfer bursts when warming tens of contiguous pages: average 700us per 1MB transferred; sustained bursts saturated a single memory channel producing 15–25% system-wide bandwidth noise.
- KV miss handling: additional software overhead (lookup, mapping, decode) adds ~200–500us per miss on top of pagefill.
- RAM vs NVMe fallbacks: pages pulled from swapback increased p99.9 by factor 3x; observed read amplification when page residency fragmented.

Key observations and root cause candidates:
1) Page fault latency dominates single-request cold miss path when many concurrent faults interleave. Kernel serializes parts of the page population which causes cascading stalls.
2) TLB/hugepage behavior: without explicit hugepage allocation, we observed many TLB misses for large-page hotsets. Enabling 2MB hugepages reduced average slowpath latency by ~20% but worsened worst-case in some fragmentation scenarios.
3) Memory channel contention: background warmup/draining that attempts to prefetch contiguous spans created microbursts that saturated a channel and amplified DMA latency for other threads — producing long tails.
4) Prefetch stride mismatch: our simple stride-based prefetcher frequently mispredicted access patterns on multi-tenant mixes, doing useless reads that increased effective BW and accelerated paging.
5) Eviction noise: aggressive eviction concurrently with warmup produced extra page churn and increased read amplification when pagebacks and repopulation collided.

Low-complexity mitigations tried in lab (and results):
- Conservative background warming with token-bucket rate limit: capped prefetch BW to 40% of a single channel. Result: p99.9 reduced from 1.1s to ~420ms during cold wave. Trade-off: longer time to fully warm the hotset.
- Opportunistic hugepage grouping for long-lived sessions: group allocations for sessions we detect as "anchored" (>= 5 requests within 15s). Result: p50 improved ~15–20%, p99 trimmed ~10%. Edge cases: fragmentation caused occasional regressions.
- Probationary TTL for newly loaded pages: newly-loaded pages were given short TTL which ramps up if reuse observed; this reduced eviction churn and reduced read amplification under mixed churn.
- Bandwidth-aware prefetch heuristics: tracked recent channel utilization and paused aggressive prefetch when utilization > 70%. Result: tail stabilization, but requires low-latency channel utilization telemetry.

Operational telemetry recommendations:
- Add per-page warmup age and initial-use timestamp to KV metrics so we can correlate p99 spikes with recent population events.
- Emit trace IDs for pagefill groups (group id when we warm 4+ contiguous pages) so we can find mispredicted prefetch groups in logs.
- Surface per-channel DMA BW and queue depth in Console dashboard; small charts tied to rollout windows would allow ops to throttle prefetch remotely.

Suggested experiments (next steps):
1) A/B on Dedicated pool: compare current lazy-load with rate-limited background-warmup for 2 weeks on low-traffic region. Measure user-visible p99 and p99.9 and cost delta.
2) Microbenchmark for different page sizes (64KB vs 256KB vs 2MB with transparent hugepage disabled) under mixed-access patterns to quantify TLB vs BW trade-offs.
3) Simulator run: extend our kv-eviction-stochastic-simulator to include prefetch bandwidth caps and pagefill serialization to predict tail under larger scale.
4) Kernel-mode research: test madvise(MADV_WILLNEED) vs explicit read-ahead vs io_uring async reads for page population to see which gives best latency/bandwidth control.

Implementation-level actionable changes to iterate quickly:
- Implement background-warmup with token-bucket cap and channel-awareness (PR prepared, see linked PR).
- Add probationary TTL + ramping logic to reduce immediate eviction of freshly-loaded pages.
- Add telemetry hooks for pagefill-group IDs and quick histograms for page population duration.

Risks and unknowns:
- Hugepages can help but increase allocation/fragmentation complexity; need to test across long-lived host lifecycles.
- BW throttling for prefetch reduces tails but increases warmup time which may be visible to users if throttling is too aggressive.
- Some kernel behaviors (e.g., page fault serialization) are black-box; we may need to engage infra/kernel team if we want to change kernel policies.

Appendix: quick troubleshooting checklist for ops when seeing KV cold tails in production:
- Confirm a recent scale-up or model-roll happened (look for host start timestamps).
- Check Console per-host "pagefill rate" spikes and per-channel DMA queue depth.
- Temporarily disable aggressive prefetching (remote feature flag) for most impacted hosts.
- If NVMe swapback reads are high, consider temporarily raising ephemeral in-memory pool for affected customers.

Notes to self / open questions:
- Can we expose per-host channel utilization without large perf overhead? Need to evaluate cost of sampling vs accuracy.
- Would it be feasible to implement a "graceful read-ahead" that yields when kernel pagefault latency increases? How invasive is that?
- Which customers can we pick for early A/B who tolerate slightly longer warmups but benefit from improved tail stability?

References / links (internal):
- CON-7241: cold-start KV playbook (working doc)
- PR 2048: experiment branch with bandwidth-aware-warmup
- JIRA-RT-891: p99.9 spike incident timeline

End of diary entry.

Author: Aisha Patel (eng-serving-runtime)
Reviewed: Miguel Ramirez, Katherine Zhou
